beats.lead: Neptune is the only planet ever found by doing the maths first.
beats.text: Every other planet was spotted by someone looking through a telescope. Neptune was found because astronomers calculated exactly where it had to be before anyone pointed a telescope at it.
beats.note: It remains the only planet discovered by prediction rather than direct observation.

beats.text: The clue was Uranus. Its orbit kept drifting slightly off from where the mathematics of gravity said it should be, as if something unseen was tugging on it.
beats.note: French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier worked out the position of a planet that would explain the drift. English astronomer John Couch Adams reached a similar answer independently, but his calculation went unpublished.

beats.context: roughly how close Le Verrier's predicted position was to where Neptune was actually found, an extraordinary level of accuracy for a planet nobody had ever seen.

beats.name: Johann Galle and Heinrich Louis d'Arrest
beats.role: at the Berlin Observatory, pointed a telescope at Le Verrier's predicted coordinates on the night of 23 September and found Neptune within hours.

beats.text: Adams and Le Verrier's competing claims to the discovery turned into a genuine dispute between Britain and France over who deserved the credit, one that took years to settle into the shared recognition both men now receive.

beats.line: The last planet found the old way was Uranus. Neptune was found by algebra.
